planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this is the wild straight species from which the compact Golden Fleece cultivar was selected, so expect a looser, taller habit with the same heart-shaped basal foliage.

directions: Plant divisions in well-drained, average soil in full sun to partial shade. Autumn goldenrod forms a low rosette of glossy, heart-shaped basal leaves topped from late summer into fall by arching, one-sided sprays of small golden-yellow flowers, a looser and taller counterpart to its well-known compact selection Golden Fleece. It is native to rocky wooded slopes, ledges, and calcareous outcrops of the Appalachian region from Virginia and West Virginia south to Georgia and Alabama, and spreads gradually by short rhizomes and stolons to form an attractive semi-evergreen groundcover. Like other goldenrods, its heavy, insect-carried pollen does not cause hay fever, and its late bloom period makes it an important nectar source for native bees and migrating butterflies.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Rocky Mountain Goldenrod (Northern Goldenrod, Alpine Goldenrod)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this dwarf, high-elevation goldenrod blooms much earlier than most of its relatives and needs sharp drainage rather than the rich soil many perennials prefer.

directions: Plant in gritty, well-drained, lean soil in full sun. Rocky Mountain goldenrod is a dwarf, tidy species with fringed, hairy-margined petioles and a dense, elongated cluster of golden-yellow flowers held on a short, mostly unbranched stem, blooming in early to mid summer rather than fall like most goldenrods. It is native to alpine and subalpine slopes, rocky meadows, and tundra across a huge range spanning Alaska and Canada south through the Rocky Mountains to New Mexico and into the mountains of the northeastern United States. Its compact size and preference for sharp drainage make it well suited to rock gardens and alpine plantings, and its flowers are visited by native bees and butterflies during a season when few other goldenrods are yet in bloom.
sources: Plant Select (Colorado State University / Denver Botanic Gardens)

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun; tolerates heavy clay, gravelly, or sandy prairie soils and is very drought tolerant once established.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to lean soil in full sun. Velvety goldenrod takes its name from the dense, soft pubescence covering its grayish-green stems and leaves, giving the whole plant a distinctive silvery, felted texture that sets it apart from smoother-leaved goldenrod species. It is native to the Great Plains, from the Canadian prairie provinces south to Texas and New Mexico, where it grows on dry to moist prairies, bluffs, and open woodland edges in heavier clay or sandy-gravelly soils. Compact clusters of golden-yellow flowers appear from midsummer into fall, providing late-season nectar for native bees and butterflies, and its drought tolerance and tidy stature make it a good fit for lean-soil prairie and xeric plantings.

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, sandy, acidic soil in full sun; adapted to lean, dry sites and does not need supplemental fertility.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or acidic soil in full sun. Downy goldenrod bears upright, leafy stems densely covered in fine hairs that give the plant a soft, downy appearance and are often tinged reddish or yellow, topped by dense, bottlebrush-like spikes of some of the largest individual flowers in the genus. It is native to eastern North America from Nova Scotia and Ontario south to Florida and Louisiana, favoring dry sandy plains, pine barrens, rocky ridges, and open woodland margins, though it also tolerates damp acidic soils in bogs and wet meadows. Blooming from midsummer into fall, it is a valuable, drought-tolerant nectar source for native bees and butterflies in lean, sandy garden sites where richer soil would encourage flopping.

planting.note: Plant divisions in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; unlike most sun-loving goldenrods, this species is a woodland plant that resents hot, dry, exposed sites.

directions: Plant in cool, moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade. Large-leaved goldenrod stands apart from most of its sun-loving relatives by thriving as an understory plant in cool, undisturbed forests, bearing notably broad basal leaves, up to ten inches long, and fewer but larger flower heads in a loose, elongated cluster. It is native to eastern and central Canada, from Ontario to Newfoundland and Labrador, and into the mountains of the northeastern United States, where it grows along shaded wood margins and forest clearings, blooming somewhat earlier in the season than most fall goldenrods. It provides valuable late-summer nectar for woodland-edge pollinators and is a good choice for naturalized shade gardens where few other goldenrods will perform.

planting.note: Plant divisions in thin, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; this glade specialist is adapted to shallow limestone soils that are seasonally wet and extremely dry in summer, and it dislikes rich, deep garden soil.

directions: Plant in thin, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun. Gattinger's goldenrod is a limestone glade specialist named for the nineteenth-century Tennessee botanist Augustin Gattinger, producing branched clusters that can carry over two hundred small golden-yellow flower heads in late summer. It is native to the cedar glades and barrens of the Nashville Basin in Tennessee as well as disjunct populations in the Ozark region of Missouri and Arkansas, growing in the shallow, rocky soil over exposed limestone that defines these unique glade habitats. Because it is adapted to extreme seasonal swings between winter wetness and summer drought on thin glade soil, it performs best in lean, sharply drained garden conditions rather than fertile beds, and it offers late-season forage for native bees in an otherwise harsh habitat.
sources: Tennessee Department of Environment and Conservation

planting.note: Plant divisions in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun; this Appalachian native is at home along open rocky woodland edges and dry ridges at higher elevations.

directions: Plant in well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full sun. Roan Mountain goldenrod is named for the mountain straddling the Tennessee-North Carolina border and produces narrow, upright racemes of bright yellow flowers in late summer above a branching underground caudex. It is native to the Appalachian Mountains from Pennsylvania south to Georgia and Alabama, where it grows in open rocky clearings, dry ridges, woodland edges, and roadbanks, typically at higher elevations than many other eastern goldenrods. Its tolerance of partial shade and rocky, well-drained sites makes it a good option for woodland-edge and native rock garden plantings, and it supplies valuable late-season nectar for native bees and butterflies.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in well-drained, average soil in full sun; this sterile intergeneric hybrid forms a neat, well-branched clump and will not self-seed or spread aggressively like straight goldenrod species.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average garden soil in full sun. Lemore is a cultivar of Solidaster, an intergeneric hybrid first raised in 1910 at a French nursery near Lyon by crossing goldenrod (Solidago canadensis) with the goldenrod relative now classified as Solidago ptarmicoides; the cross combines goldenrod's branching flower sprays with smaller, paler, aster-like daisy flowers. It is sterile and clump-forming rather than spreading, producing well-branched stems topped with masses of tiny flowers that open rich yellow and fade to soft lemon, and it is grown far more often as a long-lasting cut flower than as a border perennial. Unlike the wild native Solidago species in this collection, Solidaster is a garden-origin hybrid rather than a plant found in the wild, but it shares the same insect-pollinated, non-allergenic pollen and offers a long midsummer bloom season for pollinators and flower arrangers alike.
